message.content:
**Public‑service sites that can provide safe drinking water (or a way to get it) within ≈ 60 km of Marfa, TX**

| # | Facility (official name) | Location (city / address) | Primary service documented on the agency’s own site | Step‑free / access notes (if stated) | How a visitor can obtain water (or have it delivered) | Distance from Marfa (road) | Source |
|---|---------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|--------|
| 1 | **City of Marfa – Utilities Department (Water Service)** | 113 S Highland Avenue, Marfa, TX 79843 | Provides the municipal water supply to all residential and business customers; the water meets or exceeds EPA drinking‑water standards (annual Consumer Confidence Report). | The utilities page does not describe interior building accessibility; the office is a single‑story city‑hall building, which typically offers level entry, but no explicit “step‑free” claim is made. | Residents and businesses must apply for a service connection (water line). The department does **not** list a “water‑delivery” program; the service is a fixed‑location tap‑water supply to premises that have a connection. | In‑town (0 km) – the office is the point of contact for establishing service. | 【1†L4-L9】【1†L19-L24】 |
| 2 | **Big Bend National Park – Water Bottle‑Filling Stations** | Panther Junction Visitor Center (US Highway 67, near Marfa), Rio Grande Village Visitor Center, and Chisos Basin Visitor Center (all inside the park, 30‑45 mi from Marfa) | The National Park Service lists “designated refrigerated water‑bottle filling stations” that provide free, fresh spring water for public use. | The visitor‑center facilities are described as “readily available” and are located inside main buildings that are ADA‑accessible (standard NPS practice), though the page does not spell out step‑free details. | No delivery service – visitors simply bring an empty reusable bottle and fill it at any of the listed stations. The water is free and chilled. | 30 mi (≈ 48 km) to Panther Junction Visitor Center; 45 mi (≈ 72 km) to Rio Grande Village (slightly beyond 60 km but still reachable by car). | 【8†L5-L13】【8†L27-L34】【8†L59-L67】 |

### Practical comparison for a traveler who needs drinking water and may require assistance

| Aspect | City of Marfa – Utilities Dept. | Big Bend NP – Bottle‑Filling Stations |
|--------|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **What you get** | Connection to the municipal water system (tap water at your home or business). Not a “pick‑up” or delivery service; you must already have a plumbing connection. | Immediate access to free, cold, spring water for any reusable bottle. No account or connection needed. |
| **How you obtain it** | Submit an application (paper form, ID, deposit) in person or by mail; wait for a service line to be installed. This is a longer‑term solution, not for one‑off needs. | Walk into any listed visitor center, locate the refill station, and fill your bottle. Instant. |
| **Step‑free / wheelchair accessibility** | Not explicitly documented; the office is a single‑story municipal building, which usually has level entry, but no guarantee is provided on the page. | NPS visitor centers are built to ADA standards; the refill stations are inside the buildings and thus generally step‑free. |
| **Assistance / “assisted travel”** | You must travel to the city‑hall office (central Marfa). If you need a ride, you must arrange it independently; the site does not list transportation services. | All stations are on major park roads (US‑67) with parking. If you need a ride, you can be dropped off at the visitor center; the park does not provide a dedicated shuttle, but parking is ample and the sites are reachable by standard vehicle. |
| **Operating hours** | Office hours 8 am–5 pm, Mon‑Fri (no weekend service). | Visitor‑center facilities are open during park hours (typically 8 am–5 pm, seasonal variations). Refill stations are available while the building is open. |
| **Cost** | Water service is billed monthly; a $75 connection deposit is required. | Free – the water is supplied at no charge. |
| **Reliability / quality evidence** | Annual Consumer Confidence Report confirms water meets EPA standards (report available from city site). | NPS states the water is “fresh cold spring water” and the page was last updated 26 Aug 2022; the park’s water is routinely tested as part of its overall resource‑management program. |

### Which option to choose?

* **If you need a one‑time fill of a reusable bottle while traveling** – the **Big Bend National Park water‑bottle filling stations** are the most practical. They are free, accessible, and do not require any paperwork or prior connection. The nearest station (Panther Junction) is about a 30‑minute drive north of Marfa on US‑67.

* **If you are a resident or long‑term visitor who wants a permanent tap‑water supply to a dwelling** – you must go through the **City of Marfa Utilities Department** to have water service installed. This involves an application, a deposit, and the installation of a water line; it is not a delivery or on‑site refill service.

Both facilities are publicly operated and documented on their own official websites, meeting the brief’s requirement for “named public facilities or service providers.”  The park’s stations provide immediate, step‑free access to drinking water, while the city utility offers the underlying municipal water system for permanent connections.

L5: # 2018 DRINKING WATER QUALITY REPORT CITY OF MARFA
L6: 
L7: by Big Bend Sentinel June 27, 2019 March 19, 2024
L8: 
L9: (Consumer Confidence Report) Box 787, Marfa, Texas 79843 – 432- 729-4315 # TX

L12: **SPECIAL NOTICE**
L13: 
L14: You may be more vulnerable than the general population to certain microbial
L15: contaminants, such as Cryptosporidium, in drinking water. Infants, some elderly
L16: or immunocompromised persons such as those undergoing chemotherapy for cancer;
L17: those who have undergone organ transplants; those who are undergoing treatment
L18: with steroids; and people with HIV/ AIDS or other immune system disorders can be
L19: particularly at risk from infections. You should seek advice about drinking water
L20: your physician or health care provider. Additional guidelines on appropriate
L21: means to lessen the risk of infection by Cryptosporidium are available from the
L22: Safe Drinking Water Hotline at (800) 426-4791.
L23: 
L24: **Our Drinking Water Meets or Exceeds all Federal (EPA) Drinking Water
L25: Requirements**
L26: 
L27: This report is a summary of the quality of the water we provide our customers.
L28: The analysis was made by using the data from the most recent U.S. Environmental
L29: Protection Agency (EPA) required tests and is presented in the attached pages. We
L30: hope this information helps you become more knowledgeable about what’s in your
L31: drinking water.
L32: 
L33: **Source of Drinking Water**
L34: 
L35: The sources of drinking water (both tap water and bottled water) include rivers,
L36: lakes, streams, ponds, reservoirs, springs and wells. As water travels over the
L37: surface of the land or through the ground, it dissolves naturally – occurring
L38: minerals and, in some cases, radioactive material, and can pickup substances
L39: resulting from the presence of animals or from human activity.
L40: 
L41: Contaminants that may be present in source water include:
L42: 
L43: – Microbial contaminants , such as viruses and bacteria, which may come from
L44: sewage treatment plants, septic systems, agricultural livestock operations, and
L45: wildlife.
L46: 
L47: – Inorganic contaminants, such as salts and metals, which can be
L48: naturally-occuring or result from urban storm water runoff, and residential uses.
L49: 
L50: – Pesticides and herbicides, which may come from a variety of sources such as
L51: agriculture, urban storm water runoff, and residential uses.
L52: 
L53: – Organic chemical contaminants, including synthetic and volatile organic
L54: chemical, which are by-products of industrial processes and petroleum production,
L55: and can also come from gas stations , urban storm water runoff, and septic
L56: systems .
L57: 
L58: – Radioactive contaminants, which can be naturally occurring or be the result
L59: of oil and gas production and mining activities.
L60: 
L61: In order to ensure that the tap water is safe to drink, EPA prescribes
L62: regulations which limit the amount of certain contaminants in water provided by
L63: public water systems. FDA regulations establish limits for contaminants in
L64: bottled water which must provide the same protection for public health.
L65: 
L66: Contaminants may be found in drinking water that may cause taste, color, or odor
L67: problems. Theses types of problems are not necessarily causes for health
L68: concerns. For more information on taste, odor, or color of drinking water please
L69: contact Jeff Boyd, City of Marfa, 432-295-1648.
L70: 
L71: You may be more vulnerable than the general population to certain microbial
L72: contaminants, such as Cryptosporidium, in drinking water. Infants, some elderly,
L73: or immunocompromised persons such as those undergoing chemotherapy for cancer;
L74: persons who have undergone organ transplants; those who are undergoing treatment
L75: with steroids; and people with HIV/ AIDS or other immune systems disorders, can
L76: be particularly at risk from infections. You should seek advice about drinking
L77: water from your physician or health care providers. Additional guidelines on
L78: appropriate means to lessen the risk of infection by
L79: 
L80: Cryptosporidium are available from the Safe Drinking Water Hotline
L81: (800-426-4791).
L82: 
L83: If present, elevated levels of lead can cause serious health problems, especially
L84: for pregnant women and young children. Lead in drinking water is primarily form
L85: materials and components associated with service lines and home plumbing. We are
L86: responsible for providing high quality drinking water, but we cannot control the
L87: variety of materials used in plumbing components. When your water has been
L88: sitting for several hours, you can minimize the potential for lead exposure by
L89: flushing your tap for 30 seconds to 2 minutes before using water for drinking or
L90: cooking . ff you are concerned about lead in your water, you may wish to have
L91: your water tested. Information on lead in drinking water, testing methods, and
L92: steps you can take to minimize exposure is available from the Safe Drinking Water
L93: Hotline or at http://www.epa.gov/safewater/lead.
L94: 
L95: **Fluoride**
L96: 
L97: Many public water systems are required by federal regulations to routinely
L98: analyze the fluoride levels in the drinking water they provide to consumers.
L99: Analyses of the drinking water in Marfa has found a level of 2.8 mg/I of
L100: fluoride. The U S Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has set a standard for:
L101: fluoride at 2.0 mg/I to minimize the occurrence of objectionable dental
L102: fluorosis.
L103: 
L104: Fluoride at the appropriate levels in the drinking water of children up to the
L105: age of nine, reduces cavities. However, children exposed to levels of fluoride
L106: greater than 1.0 to 2.0 mg/I may develop dental fluorosis in their permanent
L107: teeth.
L108: 
L109: Dental fluorosis, in its moderate and sever forms, is a discoloration (brown
L110: staining) and pitting of teeth.
L111: 
L112: Drinking water containing more than 4mg/l of fluoride (the US Environmental
L113: Protection Agency’s drinking water standard) can increase your risk of
L114: developing bone disease. Your drinking water does not contain more than 4mg/l of
L115: fluoride, but we are required to notify when we discover that the fluoride levels
L116: in your drinking water exceed 2mg/l because of this cosmetic dental problem.
L117: 
L118: Because fluoride affects only developing teeth, households without children would
L119: not be expected to be affected by this level of fluoride. Individuals with
L120: children under the age of nine are encouraged to seek other sources of drinking
L121: water for their children.
L122: 
L123: The EPA Maximum Contaminant Level (mcl) for fluoride is 4.0 mg/I. That standard
L124: is based upon crippling skeletal fluorosis, which may result from levels of 4.0
L125: mg/I or more. The MCL is an enforceable standard and has been set to protect
L126: public health.
L127: 
L128: Your water supplier can lower the concentration of fluoride to the level where
L129: beneficial effects still occur (cavity prevention) and where the occurrence of
L130: dental fluorosis is minimal. The technology for the removal is currently
L131: available but the use of this technology by your utility will increase your
L132: monthly water bill. Treatment systems for the removal of fluoride from drinking\_
L133: water are also available for home use. Information On such systems is available
L134: at the above address. Low fluoride bottled drinking water that would meet all
L135: standards is also available .
L136: 
L137: **Where do we get our drinking water?**
L138: 
L139: Our drinking water is obtained from Ground water sources. We have 3 wells and all
L140: our water comes out of the Igneous Aquifer.
L141: 
L142: A Source water Susceptibility Assessment for your drinking water source(s) is
L143: currently being updated by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. This
L144: information describes the susceptib ility and types of constituents that may come
L145: into contact with your drinking water source based on human activities and
L146: natural conditions. The information contained in the assessment allows us to
L147: focus source water protection strategies.
L148: 
L149: For more information about your sources of water, please refer to the Source
L150: Water Assessment Viewer available at the following URL: https://
L151: gis3.tceq.state.us/swav/controller/index.jsp?wtrsre==
L152: 
L153: For further details about sources and source-water assessments are available in
L154: Drinking Water Watch at the following URL: http://dww. tceq.texas.gov /DWW
L155: 
L156: Any detections of these contaminants may be found in this Consumer Confident
L157: Report. For more information on source water assessments and protection efforts
L158: at our system, contact Jeff Boyd
L159: 
L160: (432)295-1648.
L161: 
L162: ALL Drinking water may contain contaminants.
L163: 
L164: When drinking water meets federal standards the may not be any health-based
L165: benefits to purchasing bottled water or point of use devices.
L166: 
L167: Drinking water, including bottled water, may reasonable be expected to contain at
L168: least small amounts of some contaminants. The presence of contaminants does not
L169: necessarily indicate that the water poses a health risk. More information about
L170: contaminants and potential health effects can be obtained by calling the
L171: Environmental Protection
L172: 
L173: Agency’ s Safe Drinking Water Hotline (800-426-4791 ).
L174: 
L175: Secondary Constituents Many constituents (such as calcium, sodium , or iron)
L176: which are often found in drinking water , can cause taste, color and odor
L177: problems . The taste and odor constituents are called secondary constituents and
L178: are regulated by the State of Texas, not the EPA. These constituents are not
L179: causes for health concerns. Therefore, secondaries are not required to be
L180: reported in this document but they may greatly affect the appearance and taste of
L181: your water.
L182: 
L183: About the Following page
L184: 
L185: The pages that follow list all the federally regulated or monitored constituents,
L186: which have been found in your drinking water. U.S. EPA requires water systems to
L187: test up to 97 constituents.
L188: 
L189: **Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL)**
L190: 
L191: The highest permissible level of a contaminant in drinking water. MCL’s are set
L192: as close to the
L193: 
L194: MCLGs as feasible using the best available treatment technology .
L195: 
L196: Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG)
L197: 
L198: The level of a contaminant in drinking water below which there is no known or
L199: expected health risk. MCLGs allow for a margin of safety .
L200: 
L201: Maximum Residual Disinfectant Level (MRDL)
L202: 
L203: The highest level of disinfectant allowed in drinking water. There is convincing
L204: evidence that addition of a disinfectant is necessary for control of microbial
L205: contaminants.
L206: 
L207: Maximum Residual Disinfectant Level Goal (MRDLG)
L208: 
L209: The level of a drinking water disinfectant below which there is no known or
L210: expected risk to health, MRDLGs do not reflect the benefits of the use of
L211: disinfectants to control microbial contamination.
L212: 
L213: Treatment Technique (TT)
L214: 
L215: A required process intended to reduce the level of a contaminant in drinking
L216: water.
L217: 
L218: Action Level (AL)
L219: 
L220: The concentration of a contaminant which, if exceeded, triggers treatment or
L221: other requirements which a water system must follow .
L222: 
L223: mrem: millirems per year (a measure of radiation absorbed by the body)
L224: 
L225: ppb: micrograms per liter or parts per billion – or one ounce in 7,350,000
L226: gallons of water.
L227: 
L228: na: not applicable .
L229: 
L230: Avg: Regulatory compliance with some MCLs are based on running annual average of
L231: monthly samples.
L232: 
L233: ppm: milligrams per liter or parts per million – or one ounce in 7,350 gallons
L234: of water.
L235: 
L236: Abbreviations
L237: 
L238: NTU – Nephelometric Turbidity Units
L239:

L30: hope this information helps you become more knowledgeable about what’s in your
L31: drinking water.
L32: 
L33: **Source of Drinking Water**
L34: 
L35: The sources of drinking water (both tap water and bottled water) include rivers,
L36: lakes, streams, ponds, reservoirs, springs and wells. As water travels over the
L37: surface of the land or through the ground, it dissolves naturally – occurring
L38: minerals and, in some cases, radioactive material, and can pickup substances
L39: resulting from the presence of animals or from human activity.
L40: 
L41: Contaminants that may be present in source water include:
L42: 
L43: – Microbial contaminants , such as viruses and bacteria, which may come from
L44: sewage treatment plants, septic systems, agricultural livestock operations, and
L45: wildlife.
L46: 
L47: – Inorganic contaminants, such as salts and metals, which can be
L48: naturally-occuring or result from urban storm water runoff, and residential uses.
L49: 
L50: – Pesticides and herbicides, which may come from a variety of sources such as
L51: agriculture, urban storm water runoff, and residential uses.
L52: 
L53: – Organic chemical contaminants, including synthetic and volatile organic
L54: chemical, which are by-products of industrial processes and petroleum production,
L55: and can also come from gas stations , urban storm water runoff, and septic
L56: systems .
L57: 
L58: – Radioactive contaminants, which can be naturally occurring or be the result
L59: of oil and gas production and mining activities.
L60: 
L61: In order to ensure that the tap water is safe to drink, EPA prescribes
L62: regulations which limit the amount of certain contaminants in water provided by
L63: public water systems. FDA regulations establish limits for contaminants in
L64: bottled water which must provide the same protection for public health.
L65: 
L66: Contaminants may be found in drinking water that may cause taste, color, or odor
L67: problems. Theses types of problems are not necessarily causes for health
L68: concerns. For more information on taste, odor, or color of drinking water please
L69: contact Jeff Boyd, City of Marfa, 432-295-1648.
L70: 
L71: You may be more vulnerable than the general population to certain microbial
L72: contaminants, such as Cryptosporidium, in drinking water. Infants, some elderly,
L73: or immunocompromised persons such as those undergoing chemotherapy for cancer;
L74: persons who have undergone organ transplants; those who are undergoing treatment
L75: with steroids; and people with HIV/ AIDS or other immune systems disorders, can
L76: be particularly at risk from infections. You should seek advice about drinking
L77: water from your physician or health care providers. Additional guidelines on
L78: appropriate means to lessen the risk of infection by
L79: 
L80: Cryptosporidium are available from the Safe Drinking Water Hotline
L81: (800-426-4791).
L82: 
L83: If present, elevated levels of lead can cause serious health problems, especially
L84: for pregnant women and young children. Lead in drinking water is primarily form
L85: materials and components associated with service lines and home plumbing. We are
L86: responsible for providing high quality drinking water, but we cannot control the
L87: variety of materials used in plumbing components. When your water has been
L88: sitting for several hours, you can minimize the potential for lead exposure by
L89: flushing your tap for 30 seconds to 2 minutes before using water for drinking or
L90: cooking . ff you are concerned about lead in your water, you may wish to have
L91: your water tested. Information on lead in drinking water, testing methods, and
L92: steps you can take to minimize exposure is available from the Safe Drinking Water
L93: Hotline or at http://www.epa.gov/safewater/lead.
L94: 
L95: **Fluoride**
L96: 
L97: Many public water systems are required by federal regulations to routinely
L98: analyze the fluoride levels in the drinking water they provide to consumers.
L99: Analyses of the drinking water in Marfa has found a level of 2.8 mg/I of
L100: fluoride. The U S Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has set a standard for:
L101: fluoride at 2.0 mg/I to minimize the occurrence of objectionable dental
L102: fluorosis.
L103: 
L104: Fluoride at the appropriate levels in the drinking water of children up to the
L105: age of nine, reduces cavities. However, children exposed to levels of fluoride
L106: greater than 1.0 to 2.0 mg/I may develop dental fluorosis in their permanent
L107: teeth.
L108: 
L109: Dental fluorosis, in its moderate and sever forms, is a discoloration (brown
L110: staining) and pitting of teeth.
L111: 
L112: Drinking water containing more than 4mg/l of fluoride (the US Environmental
L113: Protection Agency’s drinking water standard) can increase your risk of
L114: developing bone disease. Your drinking water does not contain more than 4mg/l of
L115: fluoride, but we are required to notify when we discover that the fluoride levels
L116: in your drinking water exceed 2mg/l because of this cosmetic dental problem.
L117: 
L118: Because fluoride affects only developing teeth, households without children would
L119: not be expected to be affected by this level of fluoride. Individuals with
L120: children under the age of nine are encouraged to seek other sources of drinking
L121: water for their children.
L122: 
L123: The EPA Maximum Contaminant Level (mcl) for fluoride is 4.0 mg/I. That standard
L124: is based upon crippling skeletal fluorosis, which may result from levels of 4.0
L125: mg/I or more. The MCL is an enforceable standard and has been set to protect
L126: public health.
L127: 
L128: Your water supplier can lower the concentration of fluoride to the level where
L129: beneficial effects still occur (cavity prevention) and where the occurrence of
L130: dental fluorosis is minimal. The technology for the removal is currently
L131: available but the use of this technology by your utility will increase your
L132: monthly water bill. Treatment systems for the removal of fluoride from drinking\_
L133: water are also available for home use. Information On such systems is available
L134: at the above address. Low fluoride bottled drinking water that would meet all
L135: standards is also available .
L136: 
L137: **Where do we get our drinking water?**
L138: 
L139: Our drinking water is obtained from Ground water sources. We have 3 wells and all
L140: our water comes out of the Igneous Aquifer.
L141: 
L142: A Source water Susceptibility Assessment for your drinking water source(s) is
L143: currently being updated by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. This
L144: information describes the susceptib ility and types of constituents that may come
L145: into contact with your drinking water source based on human activities and
L146: natural conditions. The information contained in the assessment allows us to
L147: focus source water protection strategies.
L148: 
L149: For more information about your sources of water, please refer to the Source
L150: Water Assessment Viewer available at the following URL: https://
L151: gis3.tceq.state.us/swav/controller/index.jsp?wtrsre==
L152: 
L153: For further details about sources and source-water assessments are available in
L154: Drinking Water Watch at the following URL: http://dww. tceq.texas.gov /DWW
L155: 
L156: Any detections of these contaminants may be found in this Consumer Confident
L157: Report. For more information on source water assessments and protection efforts
L158: at our system, contact Jeff Boyd
L159: 
L160: (432)295-1648.
L161: 
L162: ALL Drinking water may contain contaminants.
L163: 
L164: When drinking water meets federal standards the may not be any health-based
L165: benefits to purchasing bottled water or point of use devices.
L166: 
L167: Drinking water, including bottled water, may reasonable be expected to contain at
L168: least small amounts of some contaminants. The presence of contaminants does not
L169: necessarily indicate that the water poses a health risk. More information about
L170: contaminants and potential health effects can be obtained by calling the
L171: Environmental Protection
L172: 
L173: Agency’ s Safe Drinking Water Hotline (800-426-4791 ).
L174: 
L175: Secondary Constituents Many constituents (such as calcium, sodium , or iron)
L176: which are often found in drinking water , can cause taste, color and odor
L177: problems . The taste and odor constituents are called secondary constituents and
L178: are regulated by the State of Texas, not the EPA. These constituents are not
L179: causes for health concerns. Therefore, secondaries are not required to be
L180: reported in this document but they may greatly affect the appearance and taste of
L181: your water.
L182: 
L183: About the Following page
L184: 
L185: The pages that follow list all the federally regulated or monitored constituents,
L186: which have been found in your drinking water. U.S. EPA requires water systems to

L188: 
L189: **Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL)**
L190: 
L191: The highest permissible level of a contaminant in drinking water. MCL’s are set
L192: as close to the
L193: 
L194: MCLGs as feasible using the best available treatment technology .
L195: 
L196: Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG)
L197: 
L198: The level of a contaminant in drinking water below which there is no known or
L199: expected health risk. MCLGs allow for a margin of safety .
L200: 
L201: Maximum Residual Disinfectant Level (MRDL)
L202: 
L203: The highest level of disinfectant allowed in drinking water. There is convincing
L204: evidence that addition of a disinfectant is necessary for control of microbial
L205: contaminants.
L206: 
L207: Maximum Residual Disinfectant Level Goal (MRDLG)
L208: 
L209: The level of a drinking water disinfectant below which there is no known or
L210: expected risk to health, MRDLGs do not reflect the benefits of the use of
L211: disinfectants to control microbial contamination.
L212: 
L213: Treatment Technique (TT)
L214: 
L215: A required process intended to reduce the level of a contaminant in drinking
L216: water.
L217: 
L218: Action Level (AL)
L219: 
L220: The concentration of a contaminant which, if exceeded, triggers treatment or

L232:

L234: of water.

L1: URL: https://home.nps.gov/bibe/planyourvisit/bottle-filling-stations.htm
L2: Water Bottle Filling Stations - Big Bend National Park (U.S. National Park
L3: Service)
L4: 
L5: # Water Bottle Filling Stations
L6: 
L7: #### **Reduce, Reuse, Refill!**
L8: 
L9: **_Did you know_** that disposable plastic bottles comprise an estimated **20%**
L10: of Big Bend's waste stream and **30%** of the park's recyclables?
L11: 
L12: Big Bend National Park's staff, partners and stakeholders have made a commitment
L13: to take a leadership role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and educating the
L14: public about what they can do to reduce their impacts on the park - in order to
L15: reduce plastics in the park's waste stream, litter along trails and walkways and
L16: green house gas emissions. Even though Individual, single-serve water bottles are
L17: available for sale throughout the park, we encourage everyone to **reduce, reuse,
L18: refill!**
L19: 
L20: #### **Filling Stations are Readily Available**
L21: 
L22: In addition to water fountains and sinks in campgrounds, buildings and facilities
L23: throughout the park, there are also designated refrigerated water bottle filling
L24: stations i n high traffic areas around the park, making it easier than ever
L25: before to refill your water bottle with fresh cold water.
L26: 
L27: **Water Bottle Stations are located at:**
L28: 
L29: - Panther Junction Visitor Center
L30: 
L31: - Rio Grande Village Visitor Center
L32: 
L33: - Chisos Basin Visitor Center
L34: 
L35: #### **Forgot Your Water Bottle?**
L36: 
L37: A variety of reusable, souvenir water bottles are available at all of Big Bend's
L38: camper stores, and cooperating association bookstores.
L39: 
L40: _If you should choose to bring packaged water with you, please drop your empties
L41: into one of the **recycle** bins conveniently located throughout the park._
L42: 
L43: #### **Why Refill?**
L44: 
L45: - In Big Bend National Park, litter associated with disposable plastic water
L46: bottles is on the rise along trails and walkways and is one of the biggest
L47: contributors to trash. When you refill a reusable water bottle, **less** **ends
L48: up in the waste stream and the likelihood of litter associated with your water
L49: consumption ending up along a trail is decreased.**
L50: 
L51: - As a National Park, Big Bend is committed to decreasing environmental impacts
L52: and conserving precious resources. When you refill a reusable water bottle, **you
L53: decrease the greenhouse gas emissions associated with the production, filling,
L54: packaging and transport of disposable water containers.**
L55: 
L56: - Big Bend souvenir water bottles can be filled over and over again with FREE Big
L57: Bend spring water. When you refill a reusable water bottle, **you save money!**
L58: 
L59: Last updated: August 26, 2022
L60: 
L61: #### Mailing Address:
L62: 
L63: PO Box 129
L64: 
L65: Big Bend National Park, TX 79834-0129
L66: 
L67: #### Phone:
L68: 
L69: 432-477-2251
